records.source: וַיִּצָּעֵק֙ אִ֣ישׁ אֶפְרַ֔יִם וַֽיַּעֲבֹ֖ר צָפ֑וֹנָה וַיֹּאמְר֨וּ לְיִפְתָּ֜ח מַדּ֣וּעַ׀עָבַ֣רְתָּ׀לְהִלָּחֵ֣ם בִּבְנֵי־עַמּ֗וֹן וְלָ֨נוּ֙ לֹ֤א קָרָ֨אתָ֙ לָלֶ֣כֶת עִמָּ֔ךְ בֵּיתְךָ֕ נִשְׂרֹ֥ף עָלֶ֖יךָ בָּאֵֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And were called out [the] men of Ephraim and crossed to Zaphon, and they said to Jephthah, why did you cross over to fight against [the] sons of Ammon, and us not you called to go with you? Your house we will burn over you with fire.
pieces: The men of Ephraim were called to arms, and they crossed over to Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight the Ammonites and not call us to go along? We will burn your house over your head!"

L.1: And the men of Ephraim were called out, and they crossed over to Zaphon and said to Jephthah, "Why did you cross over to fight against the sons of Ammon and did not call us to go with you? We will burn your house over you with fire."

R.1: The men of the tribe of Ephraim gathered their army and crossed the Jordan River to the town of Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, "Why did you go to fight the Ammonites and not call us to go with you? We are going to burn your house down with you inside it!"

decisions.choice: the men of Ephraim were called out: Ephraim mustered for war, angry at being left out
decisions.reason: The same verb is used when Ephraim was called out to join Gideon's pursuit (7:23-24), and Ephraim's complaint repeats its quarrel with Gideon (8:1). Gideon calmed them with gentle words (8:2-3); Jephthah will answer them very differently. The men of Ephraim saw being left out of a war as an insult to their tribe's honor, and perhaps as a loss of their share of the spoil.

decisions.choice: crossed to Zaphon: to a town east of the Jordan
decisions.reason: The word can be the name of the town Zaphon, in the Jordan valley in the land of Gad (Joshua 13:27), or the common noun "north" with the ending meaning "toward", giving "crossed northward". Ephraim lived west of the Jordan and Jephthah east of it, so the men must have crossed the river eastward; a town on the east bank fits that better than a direction. Both readings are possible.

decisions.choice: burn your house over you with fire: a threat to kill Jephthah and his household
decisions.reason: To burn a man's house over him was to destroy him and his family together. The Philistines made the same threat to Samson's wife (14:15) and carried it out (15:6).

decisions.choice: were called to arms; Readable "gathered their army", "the Jordan River", "the town of"
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make plain that the men of Ephraim were called together as an army. Readable also names the river they crossed and says that Zaphon is a town.

records.heading: Jephthah and the men of Ephraim

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר יִפְתָּח֙ אֲלֵיהֶ֔ם אִ֣ישׁ רִ֗יב הָיִ֛יתִי אֲנִ֛י וְעַמִּ֥י וּבְנֵֽי־עַמּ֖וֹן מְאֹ֑ד וָאֶזְעַ֣ק אֶתְכֶ֔ם וְלֹֽא־הוֹשַׁעְתֶּ֥ם אוֹתִ֖י מִיָּדָֽם׃
records.gloss: And said Jephthah to them, [a] man of strife I was, I and my people and [the] sons of Ammon, greatly; and I called you, and not you saved me from their hand.
pieces: Jephthah answered them, "My people and I were in a bitter struggle with the Ammonites. I called you, but you did not rescue me from their power.

L.2: And Jephthah said to them, "I was a man of great strife, I and my people, with the sons of Ammon; and I called you, and you did not save me from their hand.

R.2: Jephthah answered them, "My people and I were having a terrible fight with the Ammonites. I called for your help, but you did not come and save me from them.

decisions.choice: a man of great strife: deep in a serious conflict
decisions.reason: "A man of strife" is someone caught up in a dispute. Here it covers both the argument Jephthah carried on with the king of Ammon (11:12-28) and the war that followed it.

decisions.choice: I called you, and you did not save me: Jephthah's reply to Ephraim's charge
decisions.reason: Ephraim said that Jephthah did not call them (verse 1); Jephthah says that he did, and they did not come. Chapter 11 does not tell of this call, so the reader has only Jephthah's word for it.

decisions.choice: from their hand: from their power
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for power or control, as often (2:14, 16, 18).

decisions.choice: rescue / come and save
decisions.reason: The verb is the one used for the judges whom the LORD raises to save Israel (2:16, 18). Balanced says "rescue"; Readable adds "come and", since the complaint is that Ephraim did not come.

records.source: וָֽאֶרְאֶ֞ה כִּֽי־אֵינְךָ֣ מוֹשִׁ֗יעוָאָשִׂ֨ימָה נַפְשִׁ֤י בְכַפִּי֙ וָֽאֶעְבְּרָה֙ אֶל־בְּנֵ֣י עַמּ֔וֹן וַיִּתְּנֵ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה בְּיָדִ֑י וְלָמָ֞ה עֲלִיתֶ֥ם אֵלַ֛י הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּ֖ה לְהִלָּ֥חֶם בִּֽי׃
records.gloss: And I saw that not you [were] saving, and I put my life in my palm and crossed over to [the] sons of Ammon, and gave them Yahweh into my hand; and why have you come up to me the day the this to fight against me?
pieces: When I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hands and crossed over to fight the Ammonites, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} handed them over to me. So why have you come up against me today to fight with me?"

L.3: And when I saw that you were not saving [me], I put my life in my palm and crossed over to the sons of Ammon, and {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} gave them into my hand. And why have you come up to me this day to fight against me?"

R.3: When I saw that you were not going to help, I risked my life and went across to fight the Ammonites. And {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} let me defeat them. So why have you come here today to fight against me?"

decisions.choice: I put my life in my palm: I risked my life
decisions.reason: To hold one's life in one's hand is to put it at risk, as in 1 Samuel 19:5; 28:21; Job 13:14. Jephthah means that he went to war alone, without Ephraim's help, at the risk of his own life.

decisions.choice: the LORD gave them into my hand: the victory came from the LORD
decisions.reason: "Gave into my hand" is the usual way Judges speaks of victory as the LORD's gift (3:28; 4:14; 7:9; 11:32). Jephthah credits the LORD, which also tells Ephraim that they have no claim on the victory.

decisions.choice: why have you come up against me: a question that is also a reproach
decisions.reason: The question is a rebuke: Ephraim stayed away from the danger but now comes armed against the one who faced it.

decisions.choice: [me]
decisions.reason: The participle "saving" has no object in the Hebrew; Literal supplies "me" from verse 2.

decisions.choice: risked my life; let me defeat them
decisions.reason: Readable gives the meaning of the two pictures (life in the palm; given into the hand) in plain words.

records.source: וַיִּקְבֹּ֤ץ יִפְתָּח֙ אֶת־כָּל־אַנְשֵׁ֣י גִלְעָ֔ד וַיִּלָּ֖חֶם אֶת־אֶפְרָ֑יִם וַיַּכּוּ֩ אַנְשֵׁ֨י גִלְעָ֜ד אֶת־אֶפְרַ֗יִם כִּ֤י אָמְרוּ֙ פְּלִיטֵ֤י אֶפְרַ֨יִם֙ אַתֶּ֔ם גִּלְעָ֕ד בְּת֥וֹךְ אֶפְרַ֖יִם בְּת֥וֹךְ מְנַשֶּֽׁה׃
records.gloss: And gathered Jephthah all [the] men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim, and struck [the] men of Gilead Ephraim, because they said, fugitives of Ephraim [are] you, Gilead, in [the] midst of Ephraim, in [the] midst of Manasseh.
pieces: Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. The men of Gilead defeated Ephraim, because the Ephraimites had said, "You Gileadites are nothing but runaways from Ephraim, living among Ephraim and Manasseh."

L.4: And Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought with Ephraim, and the men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because they had said, "You [are] fugitives of Ephraim, Gilead, in the midst of Ephraim, in the midst of Manasseh."

R.4: So Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead, and they fought against the men of Ephraim and beat them. The men of Ephraim had insulted them. They had said, "You people of Gilead are only runaways from Ephraim. You live among the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, but you do not really belong."

decisions.choice: fugitives of Ephraim: an insult saying that the Gileadites were deserters with no proper place of their own
alternatives: you Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim, living between Ephraim and Manasseh
decisions.reason: The sense of the saying is not certain. It seems to mock the people of Gilead as runaways who had fled from Ephraim and lived on the edges of Ephraim and Manasseh, not as a true tribe of their own. Jephthah himself had been driven out of his family (11:1-3), which may sharpen the insult. The Hebrew is short and hard to read.

decisions.choice: fugitives of Ephraim: the insult is turned back on those who spoke it
decisions.reason: The same words, "fugitives of Ephraim", come again in verse 5, where they are the defeated Ephraimites trying to escape across the river. The ones who mocked others as runaways become runaways themselves.

decisions.choice: Gilead, Ephraim, Manasseh: tribes on both sides of the Jordan
decisions.reason: Half of Manasseh had settled in Gilead east of the Jordan and half lay west of the river next to Ephraim (Numbers 32:39-40; Joshua 17:1-10). Ephraim and Manasseh were both sons of Joseph, so the quarrel is within one family of tribes.

decisions.choice: the Ephraimites had said; Readable "had insulted them", "but you do not really belong"
decisions.reason: Balanced names the speakers so that it is clear who said the insult. Readable says plainly that it was an insult and spells out what it seems to mean; that expansion follows one understanding of a hard saying.

records.source: וַיִּלְכֹּ֥ד גִּלְעָ֛ד אֶֽת־מַעְבְּר֥וֹת הַיַּרְדֵּ֖ן לְאֶפְרָ֑יִם וְֽ֠הָיָה כִּ֣י יֹאמְר֞וּ פְּלִיטֵ֤י אֶפְרַ֨יִם֙ אֶעֱבֹ֔רָה וַיֹּ֨אמְרוּ ל֧וֹ אַנְשֵֽׁי־גִלְעָ֛ד הַֽאֶפְרָתִ֥י אַ֖תָּה וַיֹּ֥אמֶֽר׀לֹֽא׃
records.gloss: And captured Gilead [the] fords of the Jordan against Ephraim; and it was that when said [the] fugitives of Ephraim, let me cross over, and said to him [the] men of Gilead, [an] Ephraimite [are] you? And he said, no,
pieces: The Gileadites took control of the fords of the Jordan to cut off Ephraim. Whenever one of the Ephraimites who were escaping said, "Let me cross," the men of Gilead would ask him, "Are you an Ephraimite?" If he answered, "No,"

L.5: And Gilead captured the fords of the Jordan against Ephraim. And it was, when the fugitives of Ephraim said, "Let me cross over," the men of Gilead said to him, "[Are] you an Ephraimite?" And he said, "No,"

R.5: The Gileadites captured the places where people crossed the Jordan River, so the men of Ephraim could not get home. Whenever an Ephraimite who was running away came and said, "Let me cross the river," the men of Gilead asked him, "Are you from Ephraim?" If he said, "No,"

decisions.choice: captured the fords of the Jordan against Ephraim: cut off the Ephraimites' way home
decisions.reason: The fords were the shallow places where the Jordan could be crossed on foot. Holding them trapped the beaten Ephraimites on the east side, away from their own land. Ehud and Gideon used the same tactic against Moab and Midian (3:28; 7:24); now Israelites use it against Israelites.

decisions.choice: Ephraimite: a man of the tribe of Ephraim
decisions.reason: The word can also mean someone from Ephrathah, the clan around Bethlehem (Ruth 1:2; 1 Samuel 17:12), but here, as in 1 Samuel 1:1 and 1 Kings 11:26, it means a member of the tribe of Ephraim.

decisions.choice: and it was that whenever: a scene that happened again and again
decisions.reason: The opening words describe what took place each time a fugitive came to the river, not a single event. The sentence runs on into verse 6.

decisions.choice: Whenever one of the Ephraimites who were escaping said / Whenever an Ephraimite ... came and said
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says "the fugitives" (plural) and then "to him" (singular). Balanced and Readable make the whole scene about one man at a time. Readable adds why the fords mattered.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמְרוּ לוֹ֩ אֱמָר־נָ֨א שִׁבֹּ֜לֶת וַיֹּ֣אמֶר סִבֹּ֗לֶת וְלֹ֤א יָכִין֙ לְדַבֵּ֣ר כֵּ֔ן וַיֹּאחֲז֣וּ אוֹת֔וֹ וַיִּשְׁחָט֖וּהוּ אֶל־מַעְבְּר֣וֹת הַיַּרְדֵּ֑ן וַיִּפֹּ֞ל בָּעֵ֤ת הַהִיא֙ מֵֽאֶפְרַ֔יִם אַרְבָּעִ֥ים וּשְׁנַ֖יִם אָֽלֶף׃
records.gloss: and they said to him, say please Shibboleth; and he said Sibboleth, and not he managed to speak right; and they seized him and slaughtered him at [the] fords of the Jordan. And fell at the time the that of Ephraim forty and two thousand.
pieces: they would say to him, "Then say 'Shibboleth.'" He would say "Sibboleth," because he could not pronounce the word correctly. Then they would seize him and kill him there at the Jordan fords. At that time 42,000 Ephraimites fell.

L.6: then they said to him, "Say now, 'Shibboleth.'" And he said, "Sibboleth," and he could not manage to speak [it] right. And they seized him and slaughtered him at the fords of the Jordan. And there fell at that time of Ephraim 42,000.

R.6: they told him, "Then say 'Shibboleth.'" If he said "Sibboleth," they knew he was from Ephraim, because people from Ephraim could not say the word the right way. Then they grabbed him and killed him there at the river crossing. At that time 42,000 men of Ephraim were killed.

decisions.choice: Shibboleth / Sibboleth: a test word that gave away a man's accent
decisions.reason: The two words differ only in their first sound, "sh" against "s". The people of Ephraim evidently said "s" where the people of Gilead said "sh", so asking a man to say the word showed where he came from. The word itself is an ordinary noun, meaning "ear of grain" (Genesis 41:5) or "stream, flowing water" (Psalm 69:3, 16); at a river crossing the second sense may have been in mind. What mattered was not its meaning but its sound, so both words are given as they sound, not translated.

decisions.choice: he could not manage to say it right: he was unable to make the sound
decisions.reason: The verb means to prepare or set in order; with "not" it says that the man did not get the word right, or could not manage it. The point is that the accent gave him away even when he tried.

decisions.choice: slaughtered him: killed him without mercy
decisions.reason: The verb is often used of slaughtering animals. It shows a cold execution of men who were trying to flee, not deaths in battle.

decisions.choice: forty-two thousand: a very large loss for one tribe
decisions.reason: "Thousand" is kept here, as in the census of Numbers 1. The word can also name a military or clan unit, which would give a much smaller number (see the note at Numbers 1).

decisions.choice: Shibboleth, Sibboleth
decisions.reason: Every level gives the two words in letters that show their sound, since the story turns on how they were said. Readable adds "they knew he was from Ephraim" to explain what the test showed.

decisions.choice: men of Ephraim; the river crossing
decisions.reason: Readable says "men of Ephraim" since those killed were the fighters fleeing the battle, and "river crossing" for "fords".

records.source: וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֥ט יִפְתָּ֛ח אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל שֵׁ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֑ים וַיָּ֗מָת יִפְתָּח֙ הַגִּלְעָדִ֔י וַיִּקָּבֵ֖ר בְּעָרֵ֥י גִלְעָֽד׃פ
records.gloss: And judged Jephthah Israel six years, and died Jephthah the Gileadite and was buried in [the] cities of Gilead.
pieces: Jephthah judged Israel for six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in one of the towns of Gilead.

L.7: And Jephthah judged Israel six years. And Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in the cities of Gilead.

R.7: Jephthah led Israel for six years. Then he died and was buried in one of the towns of Gilead.

decisions.choice: judged Israel: led and governed Israel
decisions.reason: As at 2:16, a judge was a leader raised up to rescue Israel and govern it, more than a judge in a court.

decisions.choice: in the cities of Gilead: buried in a town of Gilead
alternatives: in his town, Mizpah of Gilead
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has the plural "cities", which is odd for one burial place. The ancient Greek translation reads "in his city, in Gilead", which needs only a small change in the Hebrew letters; Jephthah's home was Mizpah of Gilead (11:34). The Hebrew text is kept, understood as a burial in one of Gilead's towns.

decisions.choice: six years: a short rule with no years of peace
decisions.reason: Jephthah's notice gives no period when "the land had peace", unlike Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Gideon (3:11, 30; 5:31; 8:28). His story closes with the deaths of his daughter (11:39) and of many Ephraimites.

decisions.choice: one of the towns of Gilead
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "one of the towns", since a man is buried in one place; Literal keeps the plural as written. Readable says "led" for "judged", as at 2:16.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֤ט אַֽחֲרָיו֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אִבְצָ֖ן מִבֵּ֥ית לָֽחֶם׃
records.gloss: And judged after him Israel Ibzan from Bethlehem.
pieces: After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.

L.8: And after him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.

R.8: After Jephthah, a man named Ibzan led Israel. He was from the town of Bethlehem.

decisions.choice: Bethlehem: either the town in Judah or the town of the same name in Zebulun
decisions.reason: The text does not say which Bethlehem is meant. Elsewhere Judges names Bethlehem of Judah (17:7; 19:1), but there was also a Bethlehem in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15), and the next judge, Elon, is from Zebulun (verse 11). Either is possible.

decisions.choice: Ibzan, Elon and Abdon: three short notices of leaders
decisions.reason: Like Tola and Jair (10:1-5), these judges are given only a few facts: where they came from, their families, how long they led, and where they were buried. No battles are told of them.

decisions.choice: After Jephthah; a man named; the town of
decisions.reason: Readable names Jephthah for "him" and says "led" for "judged", as at 2:16.

records.heading: Ibzan, Elon and Abdon

records.source: וַיְהִי־ל֞וֹ שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים בָּנִ֗ים וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֤ים בָּנוֹת֙ שִׁלַּ֣ח הַח֔וּצָה וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים בָּנ֔וֹת הֵבִ֥יא לְבָנָ֖יו מִן־הַח֑וּץ וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֥ט אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל שֶׁ֥בַע שָׁנִֽים׃
records.gloss: And were to him thirty sons, and thirty daughters he sent outside, and thirty daughters he brought for his sons from the outside; and he judged Israel seven years.
pieces: He had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He gave his daughters in marriage outside his clan, and brought in thirty young women from outside as wives for his sons. He judged Israel for seven years.

L.9: And he had thirty sons, and thirty daughters he sent outside, and thirty daughters he brought in for his sons from outside. And he judged Israel seven years.

R.9: Ibzan had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He let his daughters marry men from outside his family group, and he brought in thirty young women from outside the family to marry his sons. He led Israel for seven years.

decisions.choice: sent outside / brought from outside: arranged marriages beyond his own clan
decisions.reason: To "send" a daughter is to give her away in marriage, and to "bring in" daughters for sons is to take wives for them. "Outside" means outside Ibzan's own clan. By marrying his sixty children into other families he joined his house to many others.

decisions.choice: thirty sons and thirty daughters: a large and powerful household
decisions.reason: So many children meant many wives and great wealth, the sign of a man of high rank, like Jair with his thirty sons (10:4) and Gideon with his seventy (8:30).

decisions.choice: gave ... in marriage; clan / family group; young women; as wives
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say plainly that the sending and bringing were marriages. The Hebrew says "daughters" both times; Balanced and Readable say "young women" the second time, since these were not Ibzan's own daughters.

records.gloss: And died Ibzan and was buried in Bethlehem.
pieces: Then Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.

L.10: And Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.

R.10: Then Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.

decisions.choice: buried in Bethlehem: in his home town
decisions.reason: Ibzan was buried in the town he came from (verse 8). Which Bethlehem is meant is discussed there.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֤ט אַֽחֲרָיו֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל אֵיל֖וֹן הַזְּבֽוּלֹנִ֑י וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֥ט אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל עֶ֥שֶׂר שָׁנִֽים׃
records.gloss: And judged after him Israel Elon the Zebulunite, and he judged Israel ten years.
pieces: After him, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel. He judged Israel for ten years.

L.11: And after him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel, and he judged Israel ten years.

R.11: After Ibzan, a man named Elon led Israel. He was from the tribe of Zebulun, and he led Israel for ten years.

decisions.choice: Elon the Zebulunite: from the tribe of Zebulun in the north
decisions.reason: Zebulun's land lay in lower Galilee, north of the valley of Jezreel (Joshua 19:10-16). Elon is also the name of one of Zebulun's sons (Genesis 46:14; Numbers 26:26), so this judge bears an old family name of his tribe.

decisions.choice: After Ibzan; from the tribe of Zebulun
decisions.reason: Readable names Ibzan for "him", explains "the Zebulunite", and says "led" for "judged", as at 2:16.

records.source: וַיָּ֖מָת אֵל֣וֹן הַזְּבֽוּלֹנִ֑י וַיִּקָּבֵ֥ר בְּאַיָּל֖וֹן בְּאֶ֥רֶץ זְבוּלֻֽן׃פ
records.gloss: And died Elon the Zebulunite and was buried in Aijalon in [the] land of Zebulun.
pieces: Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

L.12: And Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

R.12: Then Elon died and was buried in the town of Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.

decisions.choice: Elon ... Aijalon: the names sound alike
decisions.reason: Without vowels, the names Elon and Aijalon are written with the same letters. The town seems to share its name with the judge, or the two names were linked.

decisions.choice: Aijalon in the land of Zebulun: not the better-known Aijalon
decisions.reason: The best-known Aijalon lay in the west, in the land given to Dan (Joshua 10:12; 19:42). The words "in the land of Zebulun" show that a different place in the north is meant. Its site is not known.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֥ט אַחֲרָ֖יו אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל עַבְדּ֥וֹן בֶּן־הִלֵּ֖ל הַפִּרְעָתוֹנִֽי׃
records.gloss: And judged after him Israel Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite.
pieces: After him, Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.

L.13: And after him Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.

R.13: After Elon, a man named Abdon led Israel. He was the son of Hillel, from the town of Pirathon.

decisions.choice: the Pirathonite: from Pirathon in Ephraim
decisions.reason: Pirathon was a town in the hill country of Ephraim (verse 15). Benaiah, one of David's mighty men, came from there too (2 Samuel 23:30). So after the slaughter of verse 6, a man of Ephraim leads Israel.

decisions.choice: After Elon; from the town of Pirathon
decisions.reason: Readable names Elon for "him", explains "the Pirathonite", and says "led" for "judged", as at 2:16.

records.source: וַיְהִי־ל֞וֹ אַרְבָּעִ֣ים בָּנִ֗ים וּשְׁלֹשִׁים֙ בְּנֵ֣י בָנִ֔ים רֹכְבִ֖ים עַל־שִׁבְעִ֣ים עֲיָרִ֑ם וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֥ט אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל שְׁמֹנֶ֥ה שָׁנִֽים׃
records.gloss: And were to him forty sons and thirty sons of sons riding on seventy donkeys; and he judged Israel eight years.
pieces: His forty sons and thirty grandsons rode on seventy donkeys. He judged Israel for eight years.

L.14: And he had forty sons and thirty sons of sons riding on seventy donkeys. And he judged Israel eight years.

R.14: Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons, and each of them rode his own donkey. He led Israel for eight years.

decisions.choice: riding on seventy donkeys: a mark of rank and wealth
decisions.reason: Leaders and their families rode donkeys (5:10; 10:4). Seventy sons and grandsons, each with his own mount, show a large and wealthy household. Seventy is also the number of Gideon's sons (8:30) and of Abimelech's brothers (9:5).

decisions.choice: grandsons
decisions.reason: "Sons of sons" is the Hebrew way of saying grandsons. Readable says "each of them rode his own donkey" for the seventy matching the seventy riders.

records.source: וַיָּ֛מָת עַבְדּ֥וֹן בֶּן־הִלֵּ֖ל הַפִּרְעָתוֹנִ֑י וַיִּקָּבֵ֤ר בְּפִרְעָתוֹן֙ בְּאֶ֣רֶץ אֶפְרַ֔יִם בְּהַ֖ר הָעֲמָלֵקִֽי׃פ
records.gloss: And died Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite and was buried at Pirathon in [the] land of Ephraim, in [the] hill country of the Amalekite[s].
pieces: Then Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.

L.15: And Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekite.

R.15: Then Abdon died and was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim. It was in the hills that had once belonged to the Amalekites.

decisions.choice: the hill country of the Amalekites: a district in Ephraim named after Amalekites
decisions.reason: The Amalekites were desert raiders of the south (Exodus 17:8-16; Judges 6:3), but this hill district in Ephraim bore their name, perhaps because Amalekites had once lived there. The Song of Deborah also links Ephraim with Amalek (5:14). The reason for the name is not known.

decisions.choice: the Amalekite: a singular name standing for the people
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has the singular with the article, "the Amalekite", meaning the Amalekite people as a group.

decisions.choice: the Amalekites; Readable "that had once belonged to"
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use the plural for the people. Readable adds "once belonged to" to explain the name; it is one likely reason, not a certain one.
